title: Adaptive precision journey: INT8/FP8 SLA lab
meeting_header:
Date: 2025-09-30
Start: 15:00 PDT
Duration: 58 minutes
Location: Zoom
Recording: enabled
Attendees: Maya Thompson (Redwood AE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE), Dr. Priya Kapoor (Norwood Head of ML), Samir Patel (Norwood Infra), Elena Ruiz (Norwood CTO)
summary: Redwood ran an Optimize console lab showing adaptive precision profiles for INT8 and FP8, demonstrated latency vs quality tradeoffs using Norwood's sample prompts, and walked through runtime fallback rules and SLA implications for hosted vs dedicated deployments. Customer requested sandbox access and a narrow pilot focused on latency-sensitive inference paths for triage templates.
topics: Overview of INT8 vs FP8 profiles
Console demo: profile selection and heatmap view
Live sensitivity sweep with Norwood prompts
SLA/latency targets and dedicated vs hosted tradeoffs
Next steps: sandbox, benchmark, pilot scope

transcript:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we can give a 45-60 minute lab, aiming to show adaptive precision and how you might meet tight P95s with fallback rules.
[00:12] Dr. Priya Kapoor: Thanks Maya, quick context, we run triage assistants across incoming clinician notes, latency needs to be under ~350ms P95 for in-line use. Quality must not regress on critical extraction tasks.
[00:28] Maya: Got it. Samir, do you own the infra decision between hosted and dedicated?
[00:36] Samir Patel: I do. We're trying to avoid too much ops but we also need predictable tail latency for some paths. Security is also a must, SOC2, SSO, KMS, VPC.
[00:46] Liam (Redwood SE): Quick note, Optimize supports private deployments and we can pin to a dedicated pool for guaranteed capacity. The adaptive precision feature lets you pick per-route profiles—like higher-fidelity FP8 for extraction routes, INT8 for free-text where latency is more important.
[01:05] Elena Ruiz: When you say FP8, are we talking the new F P eight microformats? How big is the quality delta vs INT8?
[01:15] Liam: Great question. It depends on the prompt distribution. In our benchmark earlier this month on a clinical extraction suite, FP8 held ~98.7% of reference F1, INT8 was around 96.1% — so roughly a 2.6 point delta on average. Latency-wise INT8 gave us ~1.8-2.2x token throughput improvement in continuous batching scenarios.
[01:40] Dr. Priya: 2.6 F1 points are significant for critical fields. Can we selectively apply INT8 only to non-critical flows?
[01:48] Maya: Exactly, that's the adaptive part. In the console demo we'll show per-route profiles and a heatmap that surfaces sensitivity.
[01:56] [02:15] -- Console share starts --
[02:18] Liam: I'm in the Optimize console now. Top-left is the model catalog, we've got your pinned model, and here are precision profiles. You can see a profile called "latency-lean-int8" and another "fidelity-fp8".
[02:36] Liam: (mis-transcribed) The heat-map shows prompt clusters by sensitivity — darker means higher quality delta when moving to INT8. For example cluster 3 (clinical-labs) looks pretty sensitive.
[02:50] Samir: Can you drill into the raw scoring? We need to see the actual answer diffs and token-level timings.
[02:58] Liam: Yep. Export -> CSV includes prompt, baseline tokens, INT8 output, FP8 output, similarity score. I'll export that now.
[03:10] [03:35] Maya: While Liam exports, a quick architecture note: runtime fallbacks can be configured by latency threshold, e.g., if INT8 path takes >250ms or token queue grows, requests auto-fallback to FP8 or a higher-capacity instance. Fallback rules can also be per-route.
[03:55] Elena: So fallback will increase cost when it triggers, right?
[04:00] Maya: Yes, cost goes up when you land on higher-fidelity variants, but that's an explicit trade-off and we surface expected unit cost impact in the console.
[04:12] Dr. Priya: What's the behavior under cold KV cache conditions? We often have cold starts for rare templates.
[04:20] Liam: Good callout. Cold KV cache can add ~30-70ms depending on sequence length. We have prefix caching and warmup hooks; also Recommend retaining a small warm pool for infrequent but critical routes.
[04:33] [04:55] Samir: For dedicated pool SLA, what's the guaranteed P95?
[05:00] Maya: Our Dedicated offering can give an SLA-backed P95 target — we usually commit to a P95 window and scale policies; exact numbers are in the contract but we can aim for sub-350ms for the routes we pin if workload geometry fits.
[05:15] Dr. Priya: Can you show a live sensitivity sweep with one of our prompts?
[05:22] Liam: Absolutely, please paste one.
[05:28] [05:45] Dr. Priya: (pastes prompt) "Extract medication name, dosage, and timing from note: 'Patient on 5 mg lisinopril qd, reports occasional dizziness.'"
[05:58] Liam: Running sweep: baseline FP8 answer, INT8 answer, similarity 0.98, latency FP8 420ms, INT8 190ms. Interesting — extraction correctness equal but tokenization trimmed in INT8 path, still OK for this prompt.
[06:20] Maya: Note FP8 latency here was 420ms due to sequence expansion and batch coalescing; INT8 hits 190ms. Since you need P95 <350ms, this single prompt would be okay on INT8 but some clusters might exceed.
[06:35] [06:58] Liam: Running bulk sweep across 200 prompts now — heatmap populates.
[07:12] (transcription glitch: "K-V cash" for KV cache)
[07:20] Liam: The heatmap shows about 14% of prompts are sensitive (score <0.95 similarity) when using INT8. Those are mostly long-context items and multi-entity extractions.
[07:36] Dr. Priya: So we could route most traffic to INT8 and set a rule: if similarity <0.95 then reroute to FP8, or pre-classify prompts that are sensitive.
[07:45] Maya: Exactly. Two options: runtime fallback or static routing with a lightweight classifier pre-check. Both are supported. Runtime fallback keeps routing simple but can add tail cost; static classifier avoids cost but requires building a tiny model.
[08:02] Elena: What's the overhead of the classifier? Latency wise?
[08:06] Liam: A simple classifier adds ~15-30ms; it's often cheaper than a fallback-triggered FP8 spike. You can also run the classifier on-edge or as a fast microservice.
[08:17] [08:40] Samir: In terms of security — how do you handle logs and PII in the sandbox? We need KMS integration and audit trail.
[08:49] Maya: For Private and Dedicated we can configure KMS/HSM integrations, and audit logs are configurable on a per-tenant basis. Sandbox will have anonymized logs by default unless you opt in.
[09:05] Dr. Priya: What's the upgrade path if INT8 shows occasional degradations in production?
[09:10] Maya: You can set gradual rollouts with canary percentages, automated regression alerts tied to your eval suite, and automatic rollback rules. The Console also surfaces quality drift vs your saved prompt sets.
[09:26] [09:50] Liam: (showing console) Here is the rollout UI — you pick percent traffic, associate a prompt set for regression checks, and define trigger thresholds for rollback.
[10:05] Dr. Priya: Can we get raw latency histograms for custom time windows?
[10:10] Liam: Yes, per model/per-route/per-precision histograms are available. We can also send token-level traces for the pilot.
[10:20] Maya: Quick note on costing: INT8 reduces GPU time per token but can increase operation counts due to more requests served; FP8 keeps higher GPU utilization per request, so per-token cost sometimes goes up or down depending on batchability. We surface cost per 1K tokens by profile.
[10:38] Elena: For billing, do you do blended pricing if some fallbacks happen?
[10:42] Maya: Billing will reflect actual variant usage; we can provide blended estimates in the spreadsheet.
[10:50] [11:10] Samir: For the pilot, we want a dedicated slice that simulates peak traffic for 2 weeks. Can you reserve a burst buffer?
[11:18] Maya: Yes, dedicated pools support burst capacity and configurable autoscaling policies. We'll provision a slice for the sandbox pilot.
[11:25] Dr. Priya: Any gotchas we should watch during pilot?
[11:28] Liam: Check prompt distribution drift, remember cold K V cash costs, keep an eye on the sensitive cluster — if it grows you may need different profile rules. Also watch under-provisioned token queueing which can inflate P99.
[11:42] [11:59] Maya: Recap: Redwood to give sandbox and benchmark sheet; Norwood to provide triage prompts and SLA targets; Redwood to run sensitivity sweep and share results; schedule kickoff.
[12:10] Elena: Sounds good. One last competitor question: how does your fallback latency compare to running Anthropic's private endpoints?
[12:18] Maya: In our tests, our adaptive precision plus fallback matched or beat basin Anthropic P95 on similar hardware due to prefix caching and lower tail variance, but specifics depend on model selection and batch patterns. We can run a direct bake-off in the sandbox if you'd like.
[12:34] Samir: Yes please.
[12:37] [12:45] Maya: Great — we'll send calendar invite for pilot kickoff. Thanks everyone.
[12:52] [13:00] (end recording)
